$comment: The words of the pages this site generates: the backlog, a story, the badges index and a badge page. The labs are plain markdown under labs/<locale>/ and are not here. English is the reference: a locale is this file translated, plus the story, cast and level text of training-universe.json, which is written in English there. Read by scripts/lib/strings.mjs.

funnel.heading: Started and completed
intro: A level is started when its first branch exists in the learner's repository, and completed when its badge was awarded.

time.heading: Time spent
intro: The median time of the learners who went through, next to the estimate each lab was written with. A figure appears once {minSample} learners are behind it, and from then on it is the time the lab page announces. Under that, the lab keeps its estimate.

byLab.heading: Lab by lab
intro: From the learners who ran **Check my work** at the end of each lab: their receipts say when each one passed.

method.heading: How the time is measured
body: Nobody is timed. The time is read afterwards, between the commits, the Pull Requests and the Pull Request comments of each repository: a lab ends when its Pull Request is merged, and runs from the end of the one before.
A break longer than {cutoff} minutes is not counted, so a learner who stops for the night adds nothing. Work done in the org leaves no trace on GitHub, which makes every figure a low estimate.
Labs 1.1 and 1.2 install the tools and create the orgs before the repository exists. They are not measured, and Level 1 is counted from Lab 1.3.
Labs that share one Pull Request are measured together.

The fastest is the fastest time somebody could have done the lab in. A figure under five minutes, or under a quarter of the median, is two labs checked in a row and is set aside. The slowest is not shown: it is somebody who was interrupted.

The time a lab page announces is this median, rounded down to five minutes, and the time of a level is rounded down to a quarter of an hour. A lab measured with others takes its share of their time, and a lab fewer than {minSample} learners went through keeps its estimate. The pages are rewritten from the figures every Monday and after every badge awarded.

badges.title: Salesforce DevOps training badges
badges.description: The learners who finished a level of the free Salesforce DevOps training with sfdx-hardis, checked by a job that read their public repository.
badges.heading: Badges
intro: Everybody who finished a level of this course and claimed it.
It is a badge, not a certification: there is no exam here. What it says is that a job read the
person's public repository and found the work.
badges.nobody: Nobody has claimed a badge yet. Be the first.

claim.heading: Claim yours
body: In VS Code: Welcome page > **Training: Level N** > **Claim my badge**. It checks the whole level
on your machine first, then opens the claim form with everything already filled in, and you tick
the three boxes and submit.
Each level also asks you to star the open source project it teaches, which the command offers to
do and the audit checks.
You can also [open a claim issue]({claimUrl}) by hand,
with your level, your Trailblazer username, the URL of your public fork and the receipt lines
printed by **Check my work**.

readFromElsewhere.heading: Reading a badge from another site

banner.heading: Put it on your LinkedIn banner
intro: [Trailhead Banner](https://thb.nabondance.me/) is one of those tools. It draws a LinkedIn cover
image from a Trailblazer username: the rank, the badge and certification counts, and the highest
sfdx-hardis training badge that person claimed here.
banner.alt: A Trailhead banner, with an sfdx-hardis training badge in the top row
outro: Type your Trailblazer username, generate the picture, and set it as your LinkedIn cover. Nothing
to install and nothing to sign in to: the badge is public and keyed by that username.

badge.heading: Badges earned by {name}

meaning.heading: What these mean
body: Each badge was awarded by a job that cloned {repository}
and re-ran every check of the level against its actual content and history. A level 2 badge also
re-ran the level 1 checks, and a level 3 badge re-ran all three.
What is verified is the work in the repository: the fields, the deployment actions, the resolved
conflicts, the pipeline configuration. What is **not** verified is the state of anybody's Salesforce
orgs. Nobody is asked for org credentials, and this is not an exam.

notCertification.heading: It is a badge, not a certification
body: There is no exam and no accreditation here. Share this page under *Featured* on LinkedIn, or as a
course. Not under *Licenses & certifications*.

cloudity.heading: Who is behind this badge
body: The course is free and open source. It is offered by [Cloudity](https://cloudity.com/?utm_source=sfdx-hardis-training&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=badge), the Salesforce
consulting company that builds sfdx-hardis and runs its own projects with it: Agentforce and Data Cloud,

banner.heading: Put it in a banner
body: The same award drawn for a row of twenty: the Cloudity mark, sfdx-hardis, and which level it is, with nothing
personal in it. One picture per level, shared by everybody who earned it, which is what makes its address worth
publishing.
[Trailhead Banner](https://thb.nabondance.me/) reads it from the record: type your Trailblazer
username and it draws a LinkedIn cover with your rank, your badge and certification counts, and the
highest badge you claimed here. Generate it, then set it as your LinkedIn cover.
